1 Introduction

Principles of Access to Work

Above and beyond a reasonable adjustment

Support that complements but does not replace or subsidise an employer’s legal duty to make reasonable adjustments.

Additional costs

Support that is over and above what a non-disabled person would need to do their job.

When determining whether there are additional costs or a business benefit

Consider the support required by a disabled person doing the job. Do not take into account the cost incurred by a non-disabled person doing the job.

Meeting minimum needs

Support that allows individuals to overcome workplace barriers that arise from their disability.

Value for money

Support that meets an individual’s needs in the most cost effective way for the taxpayer.

Introduction

1. Access to Work (AtW) provides support for individual needs within the workplace above and beyond the employers reasonable adjustments.

2. These instructions will help identify:

the support customers need

the support customers are eligible for

3. AtW is available for applicants who:

have a paid job

are about to start a paid job (customers can apply 12 weeks before start date)

are returning to a paid job

4. AtW recognises that people are disabled by barriers in society, not by their impairment or difference. Barriers can be physical, or they can be caused by people’s attitudes to difference, like assuming disabled people can’t do certain activities within the workplace.

5. This approach helps AtW recognise barriers that make life harder for disabled people. Removing these barriers creates equality and offers disabled people more independence, choice and control. In some cases, this may mean only slight adjustments to the working environment.

6. Eligible customers will be offered support based on their needs. This may include a grant to help cover the costs of practical support in the workplace.

Note: From 1 April 2022, all government departments are responsible for arranging workplace assessments and adjustments for their employees known as civil servants. Civil servants can no longer apply for Access to Work support including the Mental Health Support Services (MHSS).

7. Disability awareness training is available for employers and work colleagues to gain an understanding of changes they could make towards enabling customers to participate fully and flourish in the workplace.

8. AtW supports customers with a disability, illness or health condition (this includes mental health), who are:

in paid employment or self-employed

about to start employment

in need of help at a job interview with an employer

about to start a Work Trial

about to start a Department for Education supported internship or traineeship

about to start a self-arranged work experience or young person’s work experience

serving an apprenticeship

9. AtW funding:

encourages employers to recruit and retain someone with a disability, illness or health condition

offers financial help towards the extra cost of employing someone with a disability, illness or health condition

offers practical support to overcome work related barriers

10. In some cases, the employer will share the cost.

11. Extra employment costs over and above those considered as reasonable adjustments can be considered.

12. AtW advisers have access to independent holistic workplace assessors who can identify recommendations to suit the customer’s needs.

13. Advisers work with the customer and their employer if appropriate to give the necessary support.

14. Repayment of some, or all the costs, are agreed in advance.

15. Repayments made under AtW are not liable for income tax.

16. All VAT queries must be signposted to HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC).

2 Eligibility

1. To receive support though Access to Work (AtW) the customer must:

be disabled, have an illness or a health condition that impacts on their ability to work

be 16 or over (there’s no upper age limit for support as long as employment is likely to continue)

have the right to work in Great Britain

be living in Great Britain

Note: Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands aren’t included for AtW support

2. Certain restrictions apply if the customer is working abroad. Support can be considered provided the job is based in Great Britain.

3. Additionally, the customer must be:

employed or self-employed or

about to start employment or

have a contract of employment or are about to start a Work Trial or

about to start a Department for Education supported internship or

about to start a traineeship or

about to start a self-arranged work experience or

about to start young person’s work experience

about to start or serving an apprenticeship

4. Customers in receipt of certain benefits are not normally able to get AtW.

5. These benefits are:

Incapacity Benefit (IB), including the award of National Insurance credits only

Employment Support Allowance (ESA) including the award of National Insurance credits only

Severe Disability Allowance

6. Exceptions to the above are where the customer:

is going for an interview, or

is starting a Work Trial, or

has a job to start, and will stop claiming when employment begins or

has a permitted work decision where AtW will consider in work support

Note: There’s no upper age limit for support as long as the employment is likely to continue.

7. Applications pending a decision of ESA cannot be delayed. If a customer is awaiting an ESA decision for permitted work to be eligible for Access to Work, we should advise the customer that they need to notify ESA of their work. We should not close or pause their application.

Note: Case Managers need to ensure they note the conversation they have had with the customer regarding this, including that they have signposted the customer to notify ESA.

8. If the customer is in or about to start paid employment, you must confirm that they will be paid at least the National Minimum Wage.

9. If the customer is a civil servant or a public servant, AtW advisers must visit the Civil servants and Public servants section in these instructions for more information about eligibility before and after 1 April 2022.

Identifying Civil Servants and Public Servants in government departments, agencies and public bodies

10. Civil Servants work in government departments and are employed by Government Ministers to deliver Ministerial or government objectives.

11. Customers working in Devolved Governments in Scotland and Wales are also no longer eligible for Access to Work support as they are usually Civil Servants. Public Servants work for government agencies and public bodies that perform a public function, but they are not directly working for the Crown or State. There are some organisations, occupations and job roles where it is very clear whether a customer is a civil servant or a public servant.

12. The lists below are not exhaustive:

Civil Servant examples Public Servant examples

Ministry of Defence The Armed Forces

Department for Work and Pensions The Police Services

HM Passport Office The National Health Service

HMRC Local Authorities

- Judges

- Magistrates

- BBC

- National Audit Office

- Parliamentary Ombudsman

- Electoral Commission

Step Action

1. Select this link: Public bodies publications - GOV.UK

2. Select the link to the most recent Public Bodies Report

3. Select and open the Excel version of the report. Identify the customer’s employer from the ‘Legislated Body Name’ in column A and check the Classification entry in column D

Arms Length Bodies (ALBs) are executive agencies, non-departmental public bodies, and non-ministerial departments.

13. The classification in column D can tell you which type of organisation an employee works for; Non-Departmental Public Bodies (NDBP), mainly employ public servants. Some historical NDBP organisations employ civil servants:

Executive Agencies employ civil servants

Non-ministerial departments employ civil servants

14. Where a customer states they are a civil servant or a public servant, their answer can be accepted as the customer is responsible for informing the Case Manager (CM) about their employment type. CMs can use the information available to help determine this, but where possible the customer must declare whether they are appointed as a civil or public servant.

15. If a customer working for a government department is unsure about their status as a civil servant or a public servant, and you are unable to identify it from the information available, you must contact the customer’s manager by email to confirm their status before their application can continue.

16. Where the customer’s status is disputed or their status as a civil servant or public servant cannot be confirmed, the CM must ask their Line Manager for support. If they are unable to establish the customer’s status, the case can be escalated to the Service Assurance Team (SAT).

17. If SAT are unable to deal with the query, then by exception they can raise a query with AtW policy team.

Definition of disability

18. Someone is disabled under the Equality Act 2010, if they have a physical or mental impairment that has a substantial, negative effect on their ability to do normal daily activities.

Refer to: Definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010 on the GOV.UK website

19. Customers meeting this definition of a disability are eligible to apply for AtW support.

20. Customers whose disability, illness or health condition does not substantially affect their normal day to day activities but has a considerable adverse effect on their ability to do their job can also apply.

21. The customer must be advised that when DWP makes a decision about disability, it is for support purposes only. This decision should not be regarded as proof that the individual would meet the Equality Act 2010 definition if tested in a court of law.

22. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers have a responsibility to make reasonable adjustments in the workplace.

Confirming disability

23. Customers are not usually requested to supply medical evidence or condition corroboration from a qualified health care professional.

24. AtW cannot be used to fund treatment for a disability or be used for diagnostic assessments for any type of disability, illness or health condition.

Initial contact stage

25. Ask for copies of any evidence or condition corroboration the customer has if:

there’s a disagreement with the customer

there’s difficulty in determining whether the effect of the customer’s disability will introduce extra costs above those of a non-disabled person doing the job

26. Tell the customer that the AtW adviser may ask for a specialist assessment to identify the support needed. For example:

technical support

ergonomic support

third sector specialist support

27. The adviser may ask for extra evidence or condition corroboration they think necessary at any time during an application in order to validate a request for support.

Drug and alcohol

28. People who are drug and alcohol dependent who do not have a primary disability or health condition fall outside the Equality Act 2010. However, where a health problem and/or a disability has resulted from their addiction and they are on a treatment programme, they are eligible to apply to Access to Work.

29. Establish if the customer is on a current treatment programme.

Note: An addiction treatment programme helps people overcome compulsive alcohol and/or drug use. The programme may take place in numerous environments, varying from residential rehab to outpatient therapy. They also range in their forms of treatment. There’s no predetermined length for addiction treatment.

30. Validation through self-declaration is sufficient evidence of being on a treatment programme. However, if doubt about eligibility or concern about fraud exists, evidence of the programme should be requested.

31. A referral for a holistic work placed assessment must be made in line with the existing AtW process.

32. AtW advisers must make applicants aware that for all areas of support (excluding mental health), their employer will be contacted ahead of the work placed assessment. This is to validate the applicant’s employment and to seek employer agreement to pay for any aids and equipment. Details of the customer’s health condition must not be divulged.

What is employment?

1. For AtW purposes, employment is:

full or part-time paid work, whether permanent, casual or temporary

a work trial arranged by DWP

work in an unsupported or supported environment

working as a councillor, elected official or appointee who has applied for a position on a public organisation’s board

work experience and self-arranged work experience

2. AtW is not available for those in:

voluntary work

training, except for training related to the customer’s paid employment and is undertaken whilst the customer is in receipt of normal wages for the job

3. To get AtW support, customers who are in work or starting work can supply one of the following:

a verbal offer of employment (check this as part of the initial employer engagement call)

a written offer of employment

a contract of employment

4. As well as one of the above, customers must be paid at least the National Minimum Wage (NMW)

See: National Minimum Wage check list on GOV.UK.

5. If during the initial contact with the customer there are doubts about the employment, ask the customer to provide supporting evidence.

6. The evidence will be considered when assessing the customer’s need for support.

7. Customers who are registered with an agency must have a job to start before they can receive support.

8. Approval cannot be given for any type of AtW support, if there’s evidence that a company is about to stop trading.

Civil servants, public servants and agency employees

9. From 1 April 2022, AtW does not fund adjustment support including assessments or equipment for civil servants with the exception of Mental Health Support Service.

Note: Public servants can continue to be considered for all support options available through AtW.

Members of the clergy

10. Applications from members of the clergy must be dealt with in exactly the same way as any other application. This is regardless of their religion.

11. The customer must be in paid employment. For example, a member of the Church of England clergy who receives a salary or stipend.

12. Some other religious denominations work on a voluntary basis. AtW is not available for voluntary workers.

13. If a customer’s employment status is in doubt, contact the employer or the religious organisations they belong to. Most contact details can be found on the internet.

What is self-employment?

1. For AtW purposes, self-employment is:

operating a business either on the customer’s own account or in partnership, or working for an employer on a self-employed contractual basis operating a franchised business on a self-employed basis

a business that satisfies the past or prospective viability tests

possessing a Unique Tax Reference number (UTR)

2. A customer is considered employed (even if they own the company) if:

they draw a salary

they pay Class 1 National Insurance contributions

3. If they pay Class 4 contributions, they are self-employed.

4. Work can be done:

from home

on their own premises

on premises owned or leased by someone else

on a travelling basis, for example a piano tuner

5. You must be satisfied that the applicant is self-employed. Do this by requesting:

a Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR). This is a ten-digit number issued by HM Revenue & Customs

accounts for an established business

a business plan of a standard acceptable to a bank or other financial institution

6. Self-employed contractors or freelancers, such as entertainers, actors who may not see themselves as being self-employed, must provide a UTR and CV to confirm their status.

7. AtW cannot pay for the costs of setting up a business such as:

standard items of equipment

support for fact-finding

going on courses, seminars or similar events

while the business is being formed

for the purposes of turnover, Revenue Grants will be considered, Capital Grants are not considered. See HMRC link BIM40451 — Specific receipts: grants and subsidies: introduction — HMRC internal manual

Company directors

8. Customers are considered employed (not self-employed), if they pay Class 1 National Insurance contributions.

9. Company directors are not entitled to the minimum wage. They don’t therefore,have to meet this eligibility condition to get AtW support.

10. Businesses must satisfy the business viability test. This is still true even if the customer is a company director.

11. The customer must provide proof that the company is registered with Companies House.

HM Revenue and Customs checks for self-employment

12. You can rely on HM Revenue and Customs treatment of the customer’s employment circumstances. This ensures consistency when determining an applicant is self-employed.

if the customer is employed, they will be taxed under PAYE rules and the employer will pay Class1 National Insurance contributions under the same PAYE rules

if the customer is self-employed, customers will be taxed under the Self-Assessment rules and have a UTR number for that purpose. Customers will be managing their Class 2/4 contributions through arrangements with the HMRC National Insurance Contributions Office

Business viability

13. It’s a requirement for a self-employed person or business owner/director seeking AtW support, to demonstrate that the business is a viable and legitimate concern.

14. To be considered viable, a business should achieve a minimum level of turnover each year in the course of normal operations.

15. This minimum level is set as the Lower Earnings Limit (LEL):

the LEL for 2026 to 2027 - £6,708

the LEL for 2025 to 2026 - £6,500

the LEL for 2024 to 2025 - £6,396

the LEL for 2023 to 2024 - £6,396

the LEL for 2022 to 2023 - £6,396

the LEL for 2021 to 2022 - £6,240

the LEL for 2020 to 2021 - £6,240

the LEL for 2019 to 2020 - £6,136

the LEL for 2018 to 2019 - £6,032

the LEL for 2017 to 2018 - £5,876

Refer to: GOV.UK Rates and Allowances for current or previous LEL. This site includes previous years rates.

Start-up period and down-turns

16. Any new application must be accompanied by a business plan. Advisers may decline any self-employment award if, in their judgement, the plan is unlikely to have any prospect of becoming viable.

17. New businesses or periods of sole trading may have an initial 3-year period of “test trading” where they do not have to achieve turnover at the LEL threshold.

18. Awards must be reviewed after the end of year 3 (when the first 2 years’ accounts would be available) with the view to achieving LEL in year 3.

19. If turnover has achieved LEL during the first 2 years of the test trading period, then a renewal award can be made for 3 years.

20. If LEL turnover has not been achieved during the first 2 years but progress has been made towards achieving it, and there are realistic prospects that turnover will reach the required level in year 3, a further award of 12 months can be made.

21. The customer must be made aware that if LEL turnover isn’t achieved in year 3 or in the 12 month award the award will not be renewed.

Note: Subject to satisfying all other criteria Case Managers should agree a 3 year award for a new business. When renewing after 3 years, customers will need to submit their accounts or tax returns so case managers can check turnover achieved in the second year of trading to determine continued business viability. Viable businesses should then have annual reviews to determine continued business viability.

22. An award must be terminated if self–employed trading or, a business previously not satisfying the viability test, fails to achieve turnover of the LEL in between annual review periods.

Note: This does not apply to test trading periods.

23. If a previously viable business fails to achieve turnover of LEL in between annual review periods, then a further award may be made for the following year. If the business then fails to turnover the LEL in that following year, then the award is terminated.

24. Periods for which an award is suspended, for example through temporary cessation of trading is disregarded. For example, bereavement.

Requalification

25. A person who receives an award for AtW on a self-employed basis which is subsequently terminated because the business does not satisfy the viability test, may not re-qualify for another self-employment AtW award for a period of 5 years from the date the customer first applied and subsequently awarded funding for support.

Note: An AtW award can be considered if the customer claims self-employment as a different type of business to their previous one and satisfies all other criteria.

VAT

26. All VAT queries must be signposted to HMRC.

Foster Carers

27. Case Managers must determine whether the applicant receives money as a salary for Foster caring, or whether the money they receive is solely for the child/children.

28. If the Foster carer receives a salary and satisfies standard AtW eligibility criteria, then they can be considered for support.

29. If the money received is for the child/children, is not considered a salary. This is considered voluntary work and AtW cannot provide funding.

Self-employed contractors and freelancers, including gig economy workers

1. Contractors and freelancers, including those customers working in the ‘gig economy’, are paid for instances of work, or ‘gigs’ as opposed to receiving a predicted monthly wage. The instances of work are usually temporary job roles rather than permanent.

2. In order to be considered as self-employed within the gig economy, a customer would normally identify as a contractor or a freelancer.

Contractor

3. Contractors:

typically work for single client at any one time, usually on the client’s premises

are hired on fixed-term contracts through recruitment agencies, or directly with the end client

work on a business-to-business basis with clients, whether through an agency or otherwise. They usually work for one client at a time, often full-time on a particular project for several months

are self-employed, and responsible for paying tax through the self-assessment process

may be a sole trader or have a limited company

have full control of what work they take on

can advertise their services to get new business

set their own working hours

Note: This list is not exhaustive

Freelancer

4. Freelancers:

usually work for a number of clients at a time, have full control of where they work, usually working from home

may be used on an ad hoc basis, or to complete a single task. They generally work for several clients at once, often on a per-hour or per-day basis

are self-employed, and responsible for paying tax through the self-assessment process

may be a sole trader or have a limited company

don’t usually have employees, but may outsource work for specific projects

determine their own rates of pay and how they charge for their work

Note: This list is not exhaustive

Eligibility

5. Applicants who are considered self-employed as a freelancer or contractor must satisfy the standard Access to Work (AtW) eligibility criteria.

6. If the support a customer needs for a contract would take them above the cap, then BAU cap rules apply. The customer will need to renew as other capped customers need to every year.

7. Customers running a business or enterprise rather than having periods of freelance or contracted work will follow BAU self-employed instructions and would not be considered for a flexible application

Evidence

8. Customers working multiple periods of employment as either a contractor or freelancer will not follow the standard self-employed customer journey as many are unable to provide evidence of a viable business in order to make a successful application to AtW.

9. If the customer considers themselves to be a contractor or freelancer and they cannot provide a business plan, they must provide the following evidence to an Advisor instead:

a Unique Tax Reference (UTR) number. This is required as confirmation that the self-employed customer is registered with HMRC

evidence of their paid work for each period of work, including start and end dates as and when they are made available by the employer. For example, an email from the contractor’s employer evidencing their period of work, a copy of a contract, invoices for agreed work, receipts from paid work. This list is not exhaustive

evidence their rate of pay meets the National Minimum Wage level. Customers in the gig economy do not need to satisfy the Lower Earnings Level (LEL) limit but must meet National Minimum Wage level. Failure to meet the National Minimum Wage level will result in the customer not being eligible for AtW support

Note: a copy of the customer’s CV detailing the customer’s work history can be requested as evidence, if available. The CV can show a history of short periods of work which supports their self-employed contractor or freelancer status.

Flexible Application

10. A flexible application for AtW support allows customers working on a self-employed freelance or contracted basis to be awarded AtW support which can be used for multiple periods of paid employment.

11. A flexible application can be offered to self-employed freelancers or contractors who are:

new AtW customers

customers reporting a change of circumstances

customers reporting a new period of work

12. AtW support can be awarded for up to 3 years using the flexible application process. This means customers can claim for support for up to 3 years without having to make a new application each time they have a new period of work.

13. Customers can only claim payment during periods they are actively working. Their flexible application is only live during paid periods of employment. During periods where the customer is not working, their award will remain dormant and payment cannot be claimed.

14. The customer’s AtW award can be documented by the customer using a workplace adjustment passport and they can share this information with their prospective employer.

Note: this is optional for the customer. Once an award has been made and documented, the customer owns the workplace adjustment passport and it is their choice whether to share the information it contains with a prospective employer.

Actions for Advisers

15. During the information gathering stage, the customer must be informed:

if a decision is made to award AtW, they will be given an appropriate length of award, not exceeding 3 years, and they don’t need to make a new application for support during this time unless their circumstances change

they must provide details of their new period of paid work each time they make a claim for payment during the award period

where their support needs change or they have a change in circumstances, they must contact AtW before attempting to claim from their existing award as this could breach their cap

where equipment has been provided as a one off cost, they are expected to take this equipment with them when leaving a job role if it will be needed to support them in their future job roles

Note: cost share does not apply to these customers. AtW would meet the cost of moving the equipment in future. See: Transferability and portability of equipment

16. To finalise the award:

Step Action

1 Access DiSC and enter the Job Title to confirm the customer has a flexible application

For example, ‘Freelance TV Producer (FLEXIBLE APPLICATION)’

2 Make sure the business case provides clear evidence to support the customer’s flexible application and award for an appropriate period

Note: three years is the maximum period of award a customer is able to claim for if they were to work every week during this period

3 Enter start and end dates for each element up to 3 years

4 Update the Business Case in DiSC and update notes for the payment officer in the element(s)

- the support in place

- details of their first period of paid work

- name of Employer/Company

For example, ‘First period of work from xx/xx/xx to xx/xx/xx – customers must provide evidence of paid work for any claims made after this date’

5 The following must be included in the customer offer letter in addition to the BAU content, to support their understanding of the flexible application process:

‘You have been given a XX year award. You do not need to make a new application each time you start a new period of paid work if your circumstances have not changed.

You do need to provide us with evidence each time you have a new period of paid work.

Where your support needs change or you have a change in circumstances, you must contact AtW.

If the support agreed has a one off cost (for example, equipment) then you would be expected to take this with you if this is still appropriate for your job’

Action for Payment Officers, first period of work

17. To make payment for the first period of work:

Step Action

1 Access ATWIS or DRS and view the correctly completed and signed claim form with all appropriate evidence.

2 Access DiSC and check the Business Case and the element notes to confirm the start and end date of the customer’s first period of paid work

3 If the claim is made within the first period of paid work

- check validity of claim form and supporting evidence

- approve the claim

- make payment

- update any relevant notes

4 If the claim includes dates not covered by the first period of work:

- payment must only be made for dates that fall within the first period of work

- reject payment for any dates outside of first period of work

- update any relevant notes

- send explanation email/letter to customer

Note: if the customer doesn’t have an email address, request the documentation from DRS and return it to customer using any agreed wording

Customer has further periods of paid work, no change of support needs

18. When the customer has their award in place, they are able to make further payment claims against this without making a new AtW application, providing their circumstances do not change. The customer must notify AtW and provide evidence of each period of paid work during the award period

Actions for Service Centre Colleagues

19. If customers contact AtW Service Centres to report a further period of paid work:

Step Action

1. Access DiSC, check DiSC notes to confirm if a flexible application note has been recorded. For example, the job title ‘Freelance TV Producer (FLEXIBLE APPLICATION)’

- check Business Case or element notes to confirm if the new period of work has already been recorded

2. Tell the customer you will arrange for an Advisor to contact them

3. Complete a Hand Over Template about the next period of paid work and send for allocation to an Advisor

Actions for Advisors

20. Customers must send evidence of any periods of paid work they wish to claim AtW support payment for. The period of work can be reported by the customer:

through the Service Centre

by email (if this is their preferred method of contact, or

by sending evidence with their payment claim form

See: Evidence

Advisor receives email from customer – preferred method of contact

21. If you receive evidence of another period of paid work from a contractor or freelancer by email, forward the email to an Allocator to allocate to an available Advisor.

Advisor notified of further period of paid work

22. If the customer reports a further period of paid work to the Service Centre, you will receive this as an allocation.

23. You must contact the customer to establish whether evidence is being sent in by post or by email. The customer can email evidence of the new period of work to the Advisor at this stage if this is their preferred method of contact. Do not request the claim form at this stage.

24. Customers can send evidence by post with their claim form. When evidence is received with a claim pack, Payment Officers will notify Allocators. The evidence will then be available for Advisers to view in ATWIS. This will show as a Payment Task.

25. When evidence is received in MOU without a claim form, it is scanned into ATWIS as Whitemail. An Allocator will allocate this to you.

26. When evidence is received in MOU with a claim form, the post is scanned as the contents of one envelope. A Payment Officer will receive this task. If they find the period of work hasn’t been recorded on DiSC, they will send an email to an Allocator, including the envelope ID in the subject line email. You must record the period of work and reply to the Payment Officer’s email confirming they can now make payment for the period. When you reply, you must copy in the Payment Officer’s Team Leader.

27. When the customer provides their evidence:

Step Action

1. If the evidence was sent with a claim form - Access ATWIS document section

Check if the customer has provided evidence confirming their next period of paid work

2. When the customer has provided their evidence, you must check the evidence provided shows their next period of paid work

3. You must make sure details of the customer’s new period of paid work are entered in the Business Case notes, including additional notes for Payment Officers in the element.

‘Period of work from xx/xx/xx to xx/xx/xx – customers must provide evidence of paid work if any claims are made after this date’

Note: Payment Officers can only make payment for evidenced periods of work

4. If the evidence was sent without a claim form, notify the customer they can now return their claim form

If the evidence was sent with a claim form, you must reply to the Payment Officer’s email, copying in their Team Leader, to confirm they are now able to make payment for the period of work.

5. If you have a task, ask your Team Leader to un-allocate the task

Note: These steps should be repeated each time the customer notifies AtW of a further period of paid work.

Actions for Payment Officers, further period of paid work claimed and evidence received with claim form

28. Customers must send evidence of any periods of paid work they wish to claim AtW support payment for. The period of work can be reported by the customer:

through the Service Centre

by email (if this is their preferred method of contact, or

by sending evidence by post or with their payment claim form

29. This can be reported by the customer through the Service Centre, email, by post (if this is their preferred method of contact) or sending evidence with their claim form.

30. If evidence of the period of work is received with a claim form, you must check if this period has been recorded in DiSC Business Case and element notes. If it hasn’t been recorded, send an email to ask for the case to be allocated to an Advisor, including the envelope ID and “Flexible application” in the subject line.

Note: the period of work must be recorded before you can make a payment.

Step Action

1 Access ATWIS and view the payment claim form and evidence

- check the customer has signed the claim form

2 If evidence is received with a payment claim form, you must access DiSC and check if the evidence has been recorded in DiSC Business Case and element notes

For example, ‘Latest period of work from xx/xx/xx to xx/xx/xx – customers must provide evidence of paid work for any claims made after this date’

If the customer has provided evidence of paid work after the dates noted, send an email to ask for the case to be allocated to an Advisor, including the envelope ID in the subject line.

Note: The Advisor will reply to your email when they have recorded the period of work in the Business Case and element notes, to confirm you can now make payment

If the payment claim form is for the period recorded in notes, go to step 3

3 Access DiSC and check Business Case and element notes to confirm if a flexible application note has been recorded.

For example, the job title ‘Freelance TV Producer (FLEXIBLE APPLICATION)’

4 Access DiSC Business Case and element notes to confirm the start and end date of the customer’s most recent period of paid work

- check if the claim has been made within the customer’s period of award

Note: AtW support can be awarded for up to 3 years using a flexible application

5 If the claim is made within the customer’s award period and the customer has provided evidence of the period of work:

- approve the claim

- make payment

- update any relevant notes with the latest paid work period
